title: Adding, Subtracting & Beyond
description: The four operations built on understanding, not just procedures: combining and separating real objects, then strategies, place-value methods, multiplication as equal groups and arrays, division as sharing and grouping, and finally order of operations and operations with fractions, decimals and integers.

stages.overview: Putting together and taking away with real objects to 10.
goals: Combine two small groups and find how many altogether
Take some away and find how many are left

units.title: Putting Together
units.summary: Adding means joining groups and counting how many altogether.
objectives: Find one more and two more than a number to 10
Join two small groups and count how many altogether
masteryCriteria: Finds one and two more than numbers to 10

revision.notes: Revisit through play: replay one activity, retell the story, and do one hands-on task. Keep revision under 5 minutes.

lessons.title: One More, Two More
objectives: Find one more and two more than a number to 10
Join two small groups and count how many altogether
explanation: When we put two groups together, we are adding. Three apples and two more apples make five apples altogether.
One more means the next number when we count. One more than 4 is 5. Two more than 4 is 6.
To find how many altogether, push the groups together and count them all. Later, you can start counting from the bigger group: "Fiiive… six, seven."
examples: 2 ducks swim over to join 3 ducks: 5 ducks altogether.
You have 4 crayons and get 1 more: now you have 5.

story.title: Kiko's Picnic Plate
story.text: Kiko had three grapes on a plate. Tara gave Kiko two more. "How many now?" asked Tara. Kiko pushed them together and counted: "One, two, three, four, five! Three and two more make five grapes altogether."

activities.prompt: 🐤🐤 and 🐤🐤🐤 come to join. How many altogether?

thinking: Does it matter which group you count first? Try it!
If you add zero more, what happens?
speaking: Tell a grown-up a number story with your toys: "I had…, then … more came. Now I have …".

project.title: Bus Stop Adding Game
steps: Put some passengers on the bus
At each "stop" add one or two more
Count how many are on the bus now
Tell the story of the journey

mastery: Finds one and two more than numbers to 10

units.title: Taking Away
units.summary: Subtracting means taking some away and counting what is left.
objectives: Take away objects and count how many are left
Find one less than a number to 10
masteryCriteria: Solves take-away problems with objects to 10
Finds one less than numbers to 10

revision.notes: Revisit through play: replay one activity, retell the story, and do one hands-on task. Keep revision under 5 minutes.

lessons.title: How Many Are Left?
objectives: Take away objects and count how many are left
Find one less than a number to 10
explanation: When some things go away, we are subtracting. If you have 5 biscuits and eat 2, there are 3 biscuits left.
One less means the number just before. One less than 5 is 4.
To find how many are left: start with the group, move away the ones that go, and count the ones still there.

vocabulary.meaning: still there after some are taken

examples: 4 birds on a wire, 2 fly away: 2 left.

story.title: Five Little Monkeys
story.text: Five little monkeys sat in a tree. One jumped down to find a banana — four were left. Another jumped down — three were left. Mayur the peacock counted, "Five take away two is three!" Soon the monkeys came back with bananas for everyone.

activities.prompt: If you take away all of them, zero are left.

thinking: Can you take away more than you have? What happens?
How is taking away like counting backwards?
speaking: Use five toys to tell a grown-up a "taking away" story.

project.title: Five Little Ducks Puppet Show
materials: five toy ducks or paper ducks
steps: Sing "Five Little Ducks"
Each verse, hide one duck behind the hill
Count how many are left each time
At the end, bring them all back and count again

mastery: Solves take-away problems with objects to 10
Finds one less than numbers to 10

stages.overview: Addition and subtraction facts to 20, using the + − = symbols and simple strategies.
goals: Read and write addition and subtraction number sentences
Add by counting on from the larger number
Understand subtraction as finding the difference

units.title: Number Sentences
objectives: Add by counting on from the larger number
Write and read number sentences using + and =
masteryCriteria: Counts on from the larger addend
Reads and writes addition sentences with correct symbols

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: Counting On
objectives: Add by counting on from the larger number
Write and read number sentences using + and =
prerequisites: Adds small groups by counting all
explanation: Instead of counting everything from 1, start with the bigger number in your head and count on. For 8 + 3: "eight… nine, ten, eleven." The answer is 11.
We write adding as a number sentence: 8 + 3 = 11. The + sign means "add", and = means "is the same as".
You can swap the numbers in an addition: 3 + 8 is the same as 8 + 3. So always start with the bigger one — it's quicker!

vocabulary.meaning: start from a number and count forward

story.title: The Lazy Counter
story.text: Rangi had 12 marbles and found 3 more. Kiko started counting all of them from one. Rangi smiled: "Twelve is already in my head… thirteen, fourteen, fifteen!" Rangi finished first. "Counting on saves my energy," Rangi winked.

thinking: Why is it quicker to start from the bigger number?
What does the = sign really mean? Is 7 = 3 + 4 a true sentence?
speaking: Show someone how to count on to solve 15 + 3, saying each step aloud.

project.title: Dice Count-On Race
materials: two dice (or one die and number cards to 12)
steps: Roll the number card and the die
Write the number sentence
Count on from the bigger number
Record ten sums and circle the biggest

mastery: Counts on from the larger addend
Reads and writes addition sentences with correct symbols

units.title: Fact Families and Subtraction
objectives: Write the four facts in a fact family
Use addition facts to solve subtraction
masteryCriteria: Uses inverse relationships to solve subtraction

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: The Fact Family House
objectives: Write the four facts in a fact family
Use addition facts to solve subtraction
explanation: Three numbers like 3, 5 and 8 make a fact family. They live in one house and make four facts: 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 3 = 8, 8 − 5 = 3, 8 − 3 = 5.
Subtraction undoes addition. If you know 6 + 4 = 10, then you know 10 − 4 = 6 without counting.
Subtraction can also mean the difference: how many more one number is than another. The difference between 9 and 6 is 3.

vocabulary.meaning: numbers that make related addition and subtraction facts
how much bigger one number is than another

story.title: The Number House
story.text: In Number Mountains stood a little house where 2, 6 and 8 lived together. Every morning they made four different sentences: "2 plus 6 is 8! 6 plus 2 is 8! 8 take away 6 is 2! 8 take away 2 is 6!" Their neighbour, a lonely number 5, wanted to join — but 5 didn't fit their family.

thinking: Why does a fact family have four facts and not three?
What happens in a fact family with two numbers the same, like 5, 5, 10?
speaking: Explain to someone how knowing 8 + 5 = 13 helps you solve 13 − 5.

project.title: Fact Family Houses
steps: Draw a house with a triangle roof
Write three family numbers in the roof
Write the four facts in the windows
Make houses for five different families
project.safety: Use child-safe scissors with adult supervision and keep small paper pieces away from younger children.

mastery: Uses inverse relationships to solve subtraction

stages.overview: Two-digit addition and subtraction, and early multiplication as equal groups.
goals: Add and subtract two-digit numbers using tens and ones
Understand multiplication as equal groups and repeated addition

units.title: Adding and Subtracting with Tens
units.summary: Using place value to add and subtract bigger numbers.
objectives: Add two-digit numbers by partitioning into tens and ones
Add by bridging through ten
masteryCriteria: Adds two-digit numbers without regrouping mentally

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: Split and Add
objectives: Add two-digit numbers by partitioning into tens and ones
Add by bridging through ten
explanation: Big numbers are easier if we split them. 34 + 25: split into tens and ones. Tens: 30 + 20 = 50. Ones: 4 + 5 = 9. Together: 50 + 9 = 59.
Adding tens is like adding ones, but with tens: 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens = 70.
Bridging ten: 28 + 5 — first add 2 to make 30, then add the remaining 3 → 33. Your bonds to 10 make this quick.

story.title: The Rupee Shop
story.text: Zuri bought a book for ₹34 and a pen for ₹25. "Tens first," she thought: three ten-rupee notes and two more make five tens — ₹50. "Then ones": four coins and five coins make ₹9. "That's ₹59," Zuri said before the shopkeeper had finished.

thinking: Why do we add the tens and ones separately?
Is there another way to solve 28 + 5? Which do you prefer?
speaking: Explain how you would add 45 + 33 to someone, using the words "tens" and "ones".

project.title: Shop and Add
steps: Label toys with prices between ₹11 and ₹49
Pick two items
Pay using tens and ones
Write the addition and check your total

mastery: Adds two-digit numbers without regrouping mentally

units.title: Equal Groups
objectives: Recognise and make equal groups
Write multiplication as repeated addition
masteryCriteria: Represents multiplication as repeated addition and arrays
Solves simple multiplication problems with objects

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: Groups Of
objectives: Recognise and make equal groups
Write multiplication as repeated addition
explanation: Equal groups have the same number of things in each group. 3 plates with 4 cookies on each plate are equal groups.
To find the total, we can add again and again: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. That is called repeated addition. We write it as 3 × 4 = 12, said "3 groups of 4".
An array arranges things in rows and columns: 3 rows of 4. Arrays show multiplication clearly — and you can turn them around to see that 3 × 4 = 4 × 3.

vocabulary.meaning: groups with the same number in each
find the total of equal groups
adding the same number again and again

story.title: The Fair Party Plates
story.text: Momo was setting four plates for friends. "Two ladoos on each plate," said Momo. Plate one: 2. Plate two: 4. Plate three: 6. Plate four: 8. "Four groups of two make eight," Momo said. "Everyone gets the same — that's fair!"

activities.prompt: 3 nests with 🥚🥚 in each. How many eggs?
Array: 2 rows of ⭐⭐⭐⭐. How many stars?
3 groups of 2 is the same total as 2 groups of 3.

thinking: Are 2 + 3 + 4 equal groups? Why not?
Why might multiplying be quicker than adding?
speaking: Make equal groups with toys and explain to someone how you found the total.

project.title: Array Hunt
steps: Find arrays at home: egg boxes, window panes, tiles, chocolate bars
Draw or photograph five
Write the multiplication for each
Count to check

assessment.prompt: 4 bags with 🍊🍊 in each. How many oranges?
3 rows of 3 chairs. How many chairs?

mastery: Represents multiplication as repeated addition and arrays
Solves simple multiplication problems with objects

stages.overview: Multiplication tables, division as sharing and grouping, and column methods.
goals: Understand division as sharing and grouping
Use column addition and subtraction with regrouping

units.title: Times Tables and Division
units.summary: Multiplication facts and their inverse, division.
objectives: Solve division problems by sharing and by grouping
Use multiplication facts to divide, including remainders

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Sharing and Grouping
objectives: Solve division problems by sharing and by grouping
Use multiplication facts to divide, including remainders
explanation: Division has two meanings. Sharing: 12 sweets shared equally among 3 children — each gets 4. Grouping: 12 sweets put into bags of 3 — you can make 4 bags.
Division is the inverse of multiplication. If 3 × 4 = 12, then 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Knowing tables makes division quick.
Sometimes things don't share exactly. 13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1: each person gets 3, and 1 is left over. In real life we decide what to do with the remainder.

vocabulary.meaning: share equally or make equal groups

examples: 17 children, cars hold 4: 17 ÷ 4 = 4 r 1, so 5 cars are needed.

story.title: The Boat Problem
story.text: 23 animals needed to cross the river, and each boat held 5. Kiko said, "23 ÷ 5 = 4 remainder 3, so 4 boats!" Tara shook her head. "Then 3 friends are left on the shore. We need 5 boats." The remainder mattered!

thinking: When should you round a remainder up, and when should you ignore it?
Why can't we divide by zero? Try sharing 6 sweets among 0 people.
speaking: Make up a division word problem with a remainder and explain what the remainder means in your story.

project.title: Times Table Patterns Poster
steps: Fill in a 10 × 10 multiplication grid
Colour patterns (e.g. all multiples of 5)
Write three things you notice
Use the grid to solve five division questions

assessment.prompt: 26 students in teams of 4 make 6 full teams with 2 students left over.
assessment.why: 4 × 6 = 24, so 2 students remain after making 6 full teams.

units.title: Column Methods
units.summary: Efficient written methods for larger numbers.
objectives: Subtract three-digit numbers using the column method with exchanging
Check answers using addition
masteryCriteria: Uses column subtraction with exchanging accurately
Explains exchanging with place value language

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Column Subtraction with Exchanging
objectives: Subtract three-digit numbers using the column method with exchanging
Check answers using addition
explanation: In column subtraction, line up hundreds, tens and ones. Subtract the ones first, then tens, then hundreds.

If the top digit is smaller, exchange: take one ten from the tens column and turn it into ten ones. For 52 − 27: 2 − 7 can't be done, so exchange one ten: 12 − 7 = 5, and 4 tens − 2 tens = 2 tens. Answer: 25.
Check by adding: 25 + 27 = 52. ✓ Addition and subtraction are inverses, so this always works.

vocabulary.meaning: swap one ten for ten ones (or one hundred for ten tens)
a vertical line of digits with the same place value
using the opposite operation to check

story.title: The Broken Ten
story.text: At the market, Zuri had ₹52 in five ten-rupee notes and two coins. She needed to pay ₹27. She couldn't take 7 coins from 2! So she swapped one ten-rupee note for ten coins. Now she had 4 notes and 12 coins, paid 2 notes and 7 coins, and had ₹25 left.

thinking: Why do we subtract the ones column first?
When might mental subtraction be quicker than the column method?
speaking: Teach someone column subtraction for 72 − 38, explaining the exchange step.

project.title: Base-Ten Bank
steps: Make paper "base ten" pieces
Model 342 − 167 with the pieces, exchanging physically
Write the column method alongside
Check with addition

mastery: Uses column subtraction with exchanging accurately
Explains exchanging with place value language

stages.overview: Long multiplication and division, order of operations, and operations with fractions and decimals.
goals: Add, subtract and multiply fractions and decimals

units.title: Order of Operations
units.summary: Agreed rules for which calculation comes first.
objectives: Evaluate expressions using the order of operations
Use brackets to change the order of calculation
masteryCriteria: Inserts brackets to achieve given results

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: BODMAS
objectives: Evaluate expressions using the order of operations
Use brackets to change the order of calculation
explanation: Without rules, 2 + 3 × 4 could be 20 or 14. Mathematicians agree: multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. So 2 + 3 × 4 = 2 + 12 = 14.
BODMAS reminds us: Brackets, Orders (powers and roots), Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right).
Brackets let us choose the order: (2 + 3) × 4 = 20. Division and multiplication have equal priority, so work left to right: 12 ÷ 3 × 2 = 4 × 2 = 8.

story.title: The Calculator Argument
story.text: Kiko and Nova typed 6 + 4 × 5 into two calculators. One showed 50, the other 26! Nova explained: the simple calculator worked left to right; the scientific one followed the order of operations. "That's why mathematicians agreed on one rule," said Nova.

thinking: Why is it important that everyone uses the same order of operations?
Can you write an expression that equals 24 using 2, 3, 4 and brackets?
speaking: Explain to someone why 8 − 2 × 3 is not 18.

project.title: Four Fours Challenge
steps: Use exactly four 4s and any operations and brackets
Make expressions for every number from 0 to 10 (e.g. 4 ÷ 4 + 4 ÷ 4 = 2)
Record each one
Find the hardest number and share your solution

mastery: Inserts brackets to achieve given results

units.title: Calculating with Fractions

topics.title: Adding and subtracting fractions and mixed numbers
subtopics: Adding and subtracting fractions and mixed numbers

objectives: Add and subtract fractions with different denominators
Multiply a fraction by a fraction
masteryCriteria: Adds and subtracts fractions with unlike denominators

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Adding Fractions
objectives: Add and subtract fractions with different denominators
Multiply a fraction by a fraction
explanation: To add fractions, the pieces must be the same size — the same denominator. ¼ + ¼ = 2/4 = ½ because quarters are already the same size.
For different denominators, find equivalent fractions with a common denominator: ½ + ⅓ = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Add the numerators; the denominator stays the same.
Multiplying fractions means "a fraction of a fraction": ½ × ⅓ = ⅙ (half of a third). Multiply numerators and multiply denominators.

vocabulary.meaning: a shared denominator for two fractions
write a fraction in lowest terms

story.title: The Pizza Mix-Up
story.text: Rangi ate ½ of a pizza and Kiko ate ⅓ of an identical pizza. "Together we ate 2/5!" said Kiko, adding tops and bottoms. Nova drew both pizzas cut into sixths: 3/6 and 2/6 — 5/6 altogether. "You can't add different-sized slices without making them the same size first," Nova said.

thinking: Why does multiplying by a fraction less than 1 make a number smaller?
Why don't we add the denominators?
speaking: Use a drawing to explain to someone why ½ + ⅓ = 5/6.

project.title: Recipe Scaling
materials: a simple recipe with fractional amounts
steps: Choose a recipe with fractions (e.g. ¾ cup flour)
Calculate amounts for half the recipe
Calculate amounts for 1½ times the recipe
Cook one version with a grown-up and check

assessment.prompt: Common denominator of ¼ and ⅙?
assessment.why: 12 is the least common multiple of 4 and 6.

mastery: Adds and subtracts fractions with unlike denominators

stages.overview: Operations with integers, algebraic manipulation, and estimation and error.

units.title: Operations with Negative Numbers
units.summary: Rules for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing integers.
objectives: Add, subtract, multiply and divide with negative numbers
Justify the sign rules
masteryCriteria: Justifies sign rules using models or patterns
Applies integers in contexts like temperature and finance

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Negative Numbers
objectives: Add, subtract, multiply and divide with negative numbers
Justify the sign rules
prerequisites: Places negative numbers on a number line
explanation: On a number line, adding a positive moves right; adding a negative moves left. 5 + (−8) = −3.
Subtracting a negative is the same as adding: 3 − (−4) = 7. Think of removing a debt — taking away a debt of 4 makes you 4 better off.

For multiplication and division: same signs give a positive, different signs give a negative. (−3) × (−4) = 12; (−12) ÷ 3 = −4. A pattern explains why: 3 × −4 = −12, 2 × −4 = −8, 1 × −4 = −4, 0 × −4 = 0, so −1 × −4 must be 4.

context.text: Indian mathematician Brahmagupta (7th century CE) gave explicit rules for arithmetic with negative numbers ("debts") and zero in his Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE).

vocabulary.meaning: a whole number, positive, negative or zero
a number that adds to zero (5 and −5)

story.title: Brahmagupta's Fortunes and Debts
story.text: Over 1,300 years ago, the mathematician Brahmagupta described numbers as "fortunes" and "debts". A debt minus zero is a debt; a fortune minus a debt becomes a bigger fortune. Students who imagine owing and being owed money often find his rules surprisingly natural.

activities.why: Starting at −4 and moving 9 steps right lands on 5.

thinking: Explain, using a real-world model, why subtracting a negative is the same as adding.
Use a pattern to convince someone that negative × negative is positive.
speaking: Present the pattern argument for (−1) × (−1) = 1 to someone.

project.title: Temperature Investigation

steps: Record winter minimum temperatures for 6 cities, including some below zero
Calculate the differences between pairs

Write up which calculations involved negative numbers and how you handled them

mastery: Justifies sign rules using models or patterns

units.title: The Distributive Law and Mental Strategies
units.summary: Structure behind efficient calculation and algebra.
objectives: Use the distributive law for mental calculation
Expand and factorise simple algebraic expressions
masteryCriteria: Applies the distributive law for mental calculation
Explains the law with area models

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Distribute and Factorise
objectives: Use the distributive law for mental calculation
Expand and factorise simple algebraic expressions
prerequisites: Understands order of operations and integers
explanation: The distributive law says a(b + c) = ab + ac. Multiplying a sum is the same as multiplying each part and adding.
In algebra, expanding uses the law forwards: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. Factorising uses it backwards: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3).

vocabulary.meaning: write as a product with brackets

story.title: The Speedy Shopkeeper
story.text: A shopkeeper sold 6 items at ₹199 each. Before the customer could get out a calculator, she said "₹1,194." How? 6 × 200 = 1,200, minus 6 × 1 = 6. "The distributive law is my best shop assistant," she laughed.

thinking: Why does the distributive law work? Use an area model to show it.
Is there a distributive law for addition over multiplication, a + (b × c) = (a + b) × (a + c)? Test it.
speaking: Show someone three different mental strategies for 25 × 16 and explain which is fastest.

project.title: Area Model Investigation
steps: Draw a rectangle for 23 × 14 split into 20 + 3 and 10 + 4
Find the four partial areas
Repeat for (x + 3)(x + 2)
Write a short explanation linking arithmetic and algebra

mastery: Applies the distributive law for mental calculation
Explains the law with area models
